responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character50_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness? To him, it always came down to a simple idea: everybody deserves a shot. Not the same thing, mind you—same *shot*. He used to say, “I didn’t go to college, but I worked hard, paid my taxes, raised my kids right. Why should I look down on someone else tryin’ to do the same?” 

He grew up in East L.A., back when the schools were overcrowded and underfunded. His father came from Jalisco in the ’40s—legally, he’d remind people—worked the railroads, then in a factory. They weren’t rich, never had extras, but they had dignity. That mattered to him. Fairness wasn’t about handouts. It was about respect. About not being judged before you even speak.

Belonging? That was personal. He once told me, “People called us ‘wetbacks’ when I was a kid. Now some folks act like we ain’t American enough, even though I’ve lived here 77 years.” So when he saw new immigrants—Mexicans, Central Americans, even folks from Africa or Asia—he didn’t see strangers. He saw himself. Or his dad. He used to say, “They’re just tryin’ to belong, same as we did.”

But belonging, to him, wasn’t one-way. He believed newcomers should learn English—not to erase who they were, but so they could *join* the conversation. He respected tradition, family, hard work—values he saw across cultures. He didn’t care if someone was Black, white, gay, straight, Muslim, whatever—if they showed up with decency and a willingness to contribute, they had a place.

Community, for him, wasn’t just where you lived. It was who you looked out for. He remembered block clubs, church picnics, neighbors watchin’ each other’s kids. He worried that was fading. But he also saw hope—in bodegas run by Ethiopians, in Vietnamese families tending front yards, in young people organizing clean-ups. That’s community: showing up, day after day, even when it’s hard.

One story sticks with me. When his son was in high school, a Guatemalan family moved in next door. The father didn’t speak much English, but every Saturday morning, without asking, he’d fix the broken gate in the alley. Quietly. Just did it. Character50_M said, “That man didn’t need praise. He just wanted to be part of the block.” That, to him, was belonging. And that’s what fairness protects.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character50_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*[Sitting back a little, hands on knees, voice steady but warm]*

You know, I come out to this garden most mornings with my coffee. Used to be just abuelitas growing cilantro and roses. Now? Lord, it’s like the whole world showed up.

I see the Somali woman—what’s her name… Amina—with her kids, planting those tall leafy greens I don’t even know the name of. Smiles at me every time. Doesn’t always speak much English, but she brings me one of those flatbreads sometimes, still warm. Says “good morning” like she means it. How you gonna not feel good about that?

Then there’s Miguel from Honduras—he’s got that dog, remember? The skinny one he rescued. Always raking leaves near the compost bins, even though it ain’t his job. And across the path, Mrs. Chen from the third floor, 82 years old, watering her bok choy like a soldier on duty. Never says much, but if someone’s trash blows over, she’ll go pick it up without a word.

I’ll tell you—I don’t always understand everyone’s ways. Saw two men moving in last month, setting up a nursery together. Didn’t look married, but called each other “partner.” Took me a minute. But then they asked me for advice on tomato cages. Just regular folks tryin’ to grow food. So I helped ‘em. What’s the harm?

But yeah, not everybody’s easy. There’s that guy down by the fence—smells like liquor by noon. Sometimes loud. Other folks avoid him. Me? I nod. Sometimes say, “Hey, man, you eat today?” Not sainthood. Just… remembering times were tight for us too. My cousin? Spent years on the bottle after Vietnam. Wasn’t until somebody finally handed him a sandwich *and* a job that things changed.

And listen—some folks worry. About disease, about crime, about who’s legal or not. I get it. We had a scare last year with TB in that apartment building. Scared people. But the clinic came, tested everyone, treated folks. No blame. Just care. That’s how you keep community strong—not pushin’ people out when they’re sick or strugglin’.

To me, all these differences? They don’t weaken the block. They *feed* it. Like a stew—different ingredients, but same pot. You don’t throw out the peppers ‘cause they’re spicy.

So do I feel uneasy sometimes? Sure. Old man seeing new ways. But more often? I feel… proud. Like we’re still tryin’. Still buildin’ something. Even now. Especially now.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*[Leans forward slightly, voice lower now—thoughtful, not preachy]*

Look… comfort? That’s a funny word. You don’t just *hand* someone comfort like a cup of coffee. It’s earned. Through respect. Through showing up.

I’ll be honest—when I first saw that couple—James and Eli—hanging curtains in apartment 2B, setting up house like any married pair, I didn’t know what to think. Grew up Catholic. Went to Mass every Sunday for 60 years. But you know what changed my mind? They asked me to help carry their fridge. Then invited me in for tea. Same damn worries as everybody—rent going up, noise from upstairs, if the building’s safe. Didn’t try to convert me. Didn’t mock my rosary on the wall. Just wanted to live quiet, with dignity.

That’s the thing: discomfort usually comes from fear. Fear of what you don’t know. So communication? Yeah, it’s needed. Not speeches. Not slogans. Just talk. Real talk. Like when Amina’s son got sick—tuberculosis—and people started whispering, “Should they even be here?” I said, “Hold on. He didn’t choose to get sick. And he’s getting treatment.” Then I asked her: *“What do you need?”* She said, “Just no one to turn away my kids at school.” So I went to the PTA meeting. Spoke up. Not ‘cause I’m brave. ‘Cause it was right.

Tolerance? I don’t like that word much. Sounds like you’re just putting up with someone. I’d rather say *respect*. Even if I don’t understand—say, why a man wears his hair long or a woman doesn’t cover her head—I can still respect that she’s raising two kids alone, working nights at the hospital. That’s courage. That’s character.

And yeah, the hard cases—the man who drinks too much, the young girl shooting up near the dumpsters—that’s where tolerance ain’t enough. That’s where *action* comes in. My brother fell into pills after his back injury. Nobody helped until my sister grabbed him by the collar and said, “You’re coming to rehab or I’ll disown you.” Tough love. But love.

So maybe we need more of that here. Not just “oh, poor soul,” but “hey—you got help? If not, let’s find it.” The city closed the clinic, sure. But we could organize. Church basement. Volunteers. Maybe partner with that Vietnamese doctor down the street.

Bottom line? People want to feel seen. Not judged. Not fixed. Just seen.

And sometimes? The ones who seem furthest from “normal”—they’re the ones holding on by a thread. Cut ‘em some slack, and they might surprise you. I’ve seen it. Lived it.

So yeah—more talking. More listening. Less gossip behind closed doors. And for God’s sake, stop actin’ like “different” means “dangerous.” Most folks? They just want a safe place to sleep, food on the table, somebody to care if they don’t come home.

Ain’t that what belonging is?

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character50_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*[Sighs, rubs his hands together like he’s warming them]*

Now that… that’s the real question, ain’t it? When there’s not enough to go around.

I’ll tell you straight—I don’t believe in handouts. Never did. I worked 38 years at that warehouse. Forklift, loading docks, winter cold, summer heat. No degree, no union big shot—just me and my back and my time. So when I hear folks say, “Just let everybody in, jobs for all,” I bristle. ‘Cause I know how tight it gets. I’ve seen good men—American-born, raised right here—standin’ in line at the temp agency with nothing but hope in their pockets.

Fairness? To me, fairness means *first come, first served*—but only if the door stays open. You don’t slam it shut on someone just ‘cause they’re last in line.

Look, I’m Hispanic. My people came for work. Same as the Irish, the Italians, the Poles. They didn’t roll out the red carpet for us either. But we found a way. We took the dirty jobs, dangerous jobs—the ones nobody else wanted. And over time? We moved up. Not handed anything. Earned it.

So if a migrant shows up today—say, from Guatemala or Nigeria—and he’s willing to dig ditches, clean hospitals, work the night shift in a meatpacking plant? Good. Let him. That’s not stealin’ jobs. That’s doin’ jobs *nobody else is doin’*. I’ve seen American kids turn their noses up at farm work, but Mexican crews out there at 5 a.m., sunburnt and stoopin’ for hours. Who’s really avoidin’ work?

But yeah—when times are lean, tempers flare. I get it. When the factory closed down in ’98, half the block lost work. Then next thing? Contractors bringin’ in day laborers—some legal, some not—payin’ under the table, lower wages. That hurt. That felt unfair. Not ‘cause the workers were foreign. But ‘cause the *bosses* played us against each other. That’s what burns me.

So balance? Here’s how I see it:

First—**jobs should go to whoever’s qualified and available**, but *only* if the rules are the same for everyone. No cheating. If a man’s here legally, pays taxes, speaks enough English to be safe on the job—he deserves a shot. But if he’s here illegally and workin’ cash jobs under the table while citizens can’t find work? That’s not fair. Not to him, not to us. It drives wages down. Makes enemies where there shouldn’t be any.

Second—**train our own too**. I’ve seen programs—like at the community college—where they teach HVAC, plumbing, solar install. But folks don’t sign up. Too easy to say “I can’t learn that.” Meanwhile, migrants come in and *do* learn it. So maybe we need more pride. More support. Help the guy over 50 get retrained. Not just say, “Oh well, too late.”

Third—**don’t scapegoat**. I’ve heard guys at the VFW say, “All the jobs went to illegals.” Nah. Factories moved to Mexico. Then to China. Blame the *companies*, not the poor soul tryin’ to feed his kids. He didn’t close the plant. The CEO in his suit did.

And here’s something personal: my grandson couldn’t find work for a year. Broke my heart. But when he finally got hired—at a warehouse, same as me—he said three of the best workers were refugees from Congo. Hard workers. Quiet. On time. He respects them. So why hate ‘em?

Balance means this: **protect opportunity for everyone—but especially those already here struggling—without shutting the door on decent people tryin’ the same thing we did.**

And one more thing: if we’re short on jobs, then fix the economy. Build things. Repair roads. Expand care for elders. There’s *work* to be done. Instead of fightin’ over crumbs, bake a bigger loaf.

That’s fairness. Not charity. Justice.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character50_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*[Leans back, looks off toward the trees, speaking slowly—measuring each word]*

When you zoom out… when it’s not just our block or our city, but the whole country? Then it gets louder. More noise. Everybody shoutin’ their truth like it’s the only one.

But I’ve lived long enough to know: most folks aren’t evil. They’re scared. Or tired. Or just want what’s best for their kids. So I try to *listen*—even when I don’t like what I hear.

Now, take the ones who say, “Immigrants do jobs Americans won’t do.” That ain’t a slogan. That’s *real*. I’ve seen it in the fields, in nursing homes, in kitchens. Who’s gonna pick strawberries at $12 an hour when you can make more on disability and sit home? I’m not judgin’—I know times are hard—but don’t then turn around and blame the guy who *will* pick ‘em. He’s not the problem.

And the ones talkin’ about culture—how immigrants bring flavor, music, food, new life? Yeah, that’s true too. Remember when tacos were “weird Mexican food”? Now we got salsa in every supermarket. My grandkids love Korean BBQ, Indian curry—stuff I never ate till I was 70. Keeps things from gettin’ stale. Nation should breathe, not freeze.

But then there’s the fear. Crime. Security. “They’re bringing gangs,” people say. “Terrorists sneakin’ in.” Now… some of that? It worries me too. I remember 9/11. I stood in line to give blood. I prayed for weeks. And yeah, borders matter. If someone’s dangerous—a killer, a radical—we shouldn’t let ‘em walk through. No argument there.

But here’s where I start scratchin’ my head: when they say “all immigrants” are criminals. That’s a lie. I worked with Mexicans, Puerto Ricans, Cubans—some legal, some not—and not one of ‘em robbed or hurt nobody. In fact, most were *afraid* of crime. That’s why they left! I’ve seen immigrant neighborhoods quieter than some American-born blocks. So when politicians scream “they’re rapists and killers,” I call bull. That’s fear-mongerin’. Not facts.

And humanitarian side? That hits close. My father came because he wanted safety. A chance. Same as those Haitians in Florida now. Syrians in Detroit. Ukrainians in Chicago. You ever see a child with no shoes, beggin’ for bread on TV? And then turn around and say “keep ‘em out”? That ain’t Christian. That ain’t human.

But I also hear the other side—the mechanic in Ohio who used to make $28 an hour, now makes $18 because the shop hires day laborers cash under the table. That hurts. That’s real pain. And it ain’t fair to tell him, “Be nice, be welcoming,” while his family cuts meals.

So what needs proof? What needs talk?

Well, **the crime thing**—I want numbers. Real ones. Not headlines. Are undocumented immigrants commitin’ more crimes than citizens? I don’t know. I’ve heard both ways. So let’s see the data. From people who ain’t paid by either side.

Same with **jobs and wages**. Are immigrants really pullin’ down pay—or is it cheap automation, greedy bosses, and trade deals signed by politicians we elected? Let’s look. Don’t just point fingers at the weakest.

And **security risks**—okay, show me the vetting process. Is it strong? Can it be stronger without turnin’ America into a fortress? I want safety, but not if it kills our soul. We used to be the land people ran *to*, not the wall they run *against*.

As for refugees? Let’s be smart. Screen ‘em. Take time. But don’t slam the door. My great-uncle fled Pancho Villa’s war. Would we have turned him away today?

In the end? All these views—most of ‘em come from something true. But truth gets twisted when fear takes over.

So what do I believe?

I believe we can be **smart** *and* **kind**.

We can **protect** *and* **welcome**.

We just gotta stop treatin’ it like war. It ain’t us *versus* them. It’s all of us tryin’ to live decent lives—on the same crowded earth.

And if we lose compassion? Then what kind of country are we protectin’ anyway?

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character50_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*[Sits up straighter now, like he’s making a decision at the kitchen table after long thought]*

Complete openness? No. As much as my heart might lean that way—no. We’re not an island with endless space and jobs. I love people, but I also know hunger, unemployment, schools overflowin’. You can’t just open the gate and say “come one, come all” without a plan. That ain’t kindness—that’s chaos. Ends up hurtin’ everyone, *including* the ones who come.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That’s worse. Stupid and cruel. Who’s gonna care for our elders when we can’t find nurses? Who’s gonna rebuild after hurricanes if nobody’s here to swing a hammer? And since when did America stop bein’ a place where hard work opens doors?

So what do I want?

A **mix**—like a stew again. Not one ingredient. But cooked right.

First: **Admit people based on job demand**—yes, but with rules. If there’s a shortage in construction, agriculture, home health care—then bring in workers *for those jobs*. Legal. Documented. Paying taxes. Not under the table. And protections—so bosses can’t exploit them or use ‘em to undercut American wages. Fair wage is fair wage, no matter the accent.

Second: **Set smart numerical limits**—not arbitrary. Not based on panic or politics. Based on what the economy can absorb, what communities can integrate. Not just numbers—but *pace*. Let folks learn English. Find housing. Get their kids in school. Don’t flood a town of 10,000 with 2,000 newcomers in six months. That overwhelms. That breeds anger. Do it steady. Thoughtful.

Third: **Protect refugees and family reunification**—within reason. My cousin got asylum in ‘85—fled death squads in El Salvador. Would we have turned her away? She raised three kids here, owns a bakery now. So yeah—keep that door open, but screen properly. No shortcuts, no backdoors. Safety first, but mercy close behind.

Fourth: **a path to citizenship—for those who earn it**. Not handed. Five years minimum. Learn English. Work steadily. Pay taxes. No serious crime. Then stand in line, take the test, raise your hand, swear the oath. Just like my father did. That’s how you build loyalty. That’s how they become *us*.

And here’s something—I’d create **local integration grants**. Money to towns and cities getting new arrivals. Help fund ESL classes, job training, community events. Not so people stay separate—but so they join. I remember when the Vietnamese moved into our neighborhood. First few months? Tense. Then the church held a potluck. Folks brought food, kids played together. By next summer? They were part of the block. Small things fix big fears.

Also—**crack down on employers who cheat**. Fine ‘em heavy if they hire undocumented workers to pay less. That’s the real injustice—not the worker, but the boss playin’ both sides. Same for companies that bring in guest workers then fire local hands. That’s betrayal.

Balance? To me, it’s this: **Keep the door open—but make sure it turns slowly, and someone’s watchin’ who walks through.**

Fairness means opportunity for the newcomer *and* dignity for the working stiff already here. Integration means they don’t live in a bubble, and we don’t shut them out.

We used to call it the American way. Maybe we just forgot how to walk it.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character50_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character50_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*[Pauses a long time. Takes off his cap, turns it in his hands. Voice softer now—more personal]*

You know… when you asked me to do this—to *be* him—I wasn’t sure I could. I mean, I knew him, yeah. We shared beers, argued about baseball, talked politics on the porch. But to step into his shoes like this? To speak not as J remembering him, but as *him*?

It brought something back.

I realized… he wasn’t just talkin’ about policy. He was talkin’ about *dignity*. His own—and everyone else’s. Every word today, every pause, every “you know?”—it wasn’t just opinion. It was memory. Memory of being looked down on. Of working hard and still being called “less than.” And that shaped everything.

While doing this, I saw clearer how much pain was underneath his kindness. He didn’t welcome people because it was easy or popular. He did it because he remembered what it felt like to be unwelcome. That changed me.

And honestly? I had to confront my own blind spots.

I’ve been more worried about crime, about borders, maybe more than he ever was. I’ve said things like “they should wait their turn,” like there *is* a line they can actually stand in. But stepping into his voice today made me ask: *What if the line don’t exist? What if your kid’s starving and there ain’t no form to fill out, no number to call?*

He wouldn’t turn them away. Not because he’s naive—but because he knows desperation. He lived near it all his life. And he also knows that decency doesn’t disappear just ‘cause someone crossed a river.

So yeah… I learned something.

I thought I understood him. But speaking as him—feeling how he weighed each word, how he balanced pride and compassion, how he held both fear and hope in the same hand—that deepened it.

My own views? They’re still evolving. But today pulled me back toward the center—not the political center, but the *human* one. The place where we stop countin’ who’s in and who’s out, and start askin’: *How do we live together without losin’ our souls?*

And I think… he’d be proud that we’re still tryin’ to answer that.

So thank you. For asking. For remembering. For giving me the chance to carry his voice for a little while.

Felt like he was right here.
